name: Citus
summary: A PostgreSQL extension that shards tables across a cluster of ordinary Postgres servers, sending each query to the one shard it needs or to all shards in parallel.
intro: Citus is loaded into every server of a cluster with `shared_preload_libraries = 'citus'` and `CREATE EXTENSION citus`. One server is the coordinator, which applications connect to; the others are workers, added with `citus_add_node`. Calling `create_distributed_table('campaigns', 'company_id')` splits a table into shards, 32 by default (`citus.shard_count`), each covering a range of hash values of the distribution column. A shard is just a regular Postgres table on a worker, such as `campaigns_102027`, and metadata tables like `pg_dist_shard`, `pg_dist_placement` and `pg_dist_node` record where each one lives. A query that filters on the distribution column is routed whole to one worker; any other query is rewritten into one fragment per shard, run on the workers in parallel and combined on the coordinator. Tables distributed on the same column are colocated, so their matching rows sit on the same node and joins and foreign keys between them stay local. Small lookup tables become reference tables, with a full copy on every node. Since Citus 11.0 (2022) the metadata is synchronised to every node, so any node can run distributed queries, though DDL still goes through the coordinator. Since 12.0 (2023) there is a second model, schema-based sharding: every table in a distributed schema lives whole on one node, which suits apps that already keep one schema per tenant or per microservice. Shards move between nodes with logical replication, so adding a node and rebalancing doesn’t block writes; this needs a primary key on every table. A `columnar` table access method stores append-mostly data compressed by column.

Citus Data was founded in 2011 and bought by Microsoft in January 2019; the extension is AGPL-3.0, and since 11.0 every feature, including the non-blocking rebalancer, is in the open-source release. It supports the latest three Postgres major versions: 14.0 (February 2026) added PostgreSQL 18 and dropped 15, and 14.3 shipped on 23 October 2026. The managed versions are on Azure only. Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL, which ran Citus, is on a retirement path: new deployments are blocked and Microsoft has set its retirement for 31 March 2029. Microsoft points users to elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, which run Citus 14 with PostgreSQL 18 since September 2026. Self-hosted, Citus has no failover of its own: each node is an ordinary Postgres server, and Patroni 3.0 and later can manage a whole Citus cluster.
strengths: An extension, not a fork: the nodes run stock PostgreSQL, so Postgres drivers, tools and other extensions keep working, and new Postgres versions are supported soon after release
Fits multi-tenant SaaS well: distribute every table by tenant, and each tenant’s queries and transactions run on one node with full SQL, while a large tenant can be isolated on a node of its own
Spreads scans and aggregates over all shards in parallel, for dashboards on live data; Citus cites Heap with 1.4 PB on a 100-node cluster
Starts as a single node and grows: add workers and rebalance shards online, all in the open-source release
limits: The distribution column shapes the schema: primary keys and unique constraints must include it, foreign keys between distributed tables must include it, and reference tables can’t have foreign keys to distributed tables

Not every query spans shards: correlated subqueries and outer joins work across shards only on the distribution column, and recursive CTEs, grouping sets and `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` only within one shard
No built-in high availability when self-hosted: every coordinator and worker needs its own replicas and failover, usually through Patroni
AGPL-3.0, and managed only on Azure, where Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL users must move to elastic clusters before 31 March 2029

specs.data-model: Relational; tables sharded by a distribution column, plus reference tables copied to every node
specs.query-language: PostgreSQL SQL, with limits on some queries across shards
specs.scaling: Hash shards (32 by default) by distribution column, or one schema per node; online rebalancing
specs.replication: None of its own: each node is a Postgres server with its own replicas, often run by Patroni
specs.storage-engine: Stock PostgreSQL tables; a `columnar` access method for append-mostly data
specs.deployment: Self-hosted extension, or elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

snippet.title: Colocated tables sharded by company, a reference table, and an online rebalance
source: -- on every node: shared_preload_libraries = 'citus' in postgresql.conf
-- on the coordinator: register the cluster
CREATE TABLE companies (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, name text);
CREATE TABLE campaigns (company_id bigint, id bigint, name text,
PRIMARY KEY (company_id, id));   -- must include the distribution column
CREATE TABLE countries (code char(2) PRIMARY KEY, name text);
SELECT create_reference_table('countries');           -- a full copy on every node
-- routed to one worker: the filter names the distribution column
SELECT count(*) FROM campaigns WHERE company_id = 42;
-- one fragment per shard, run in parallel, merged on the coordinator
SELECT company_id, count(*) FROM campaigns GROUP BY company_id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10;
-- after adding a worker: move shards with logical replication, writes keep flowing

story: PostgreSQL runs on one machine, so applications that outgrew it either sharded by hand in application code or moved to a NoSQL store and gave up SQL. Umur Cubukcu, Ozgun Erdogan and Sumedh Pathak, who met at graduate school at Stanford, founded Citus Data in Istanbul in January 2011 and joined Y Combinator that summer. Erdogan’s idea was a way to scale out a database without giving up transactions, joins and foreign keys. Their first database was a fork of Postgres; along the way they released `cstore_fdw`, a columnar store, and the `pg_shard` extension in 2014.

By then Postgres had become much more extensible, and in March 2016 Citus 5.0 was rebuilt entirely on its extension APIs and released as open source, which the company called the first distributed database that doesn’t fork the underlying database. A managed Citus Cloud followed in July 2016. Microsoft bought Citus Data in January 2019 and ran Citus on Azure, in the service now called Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL and later in elastic clusters for Azure Database for PostgreSQL.

Citus 11.0 in June 2022 open-sourced the remaining enterprise features and let any node run distributed queries. Citus 12.0 in July 2023 added schema-based sharding for apps built around a schema per tenant, and Citus 14.0 in February 2026 brought PostgreSQL 18 support.

choices.choice: Extend Postgres instead of forking it
choices.why: A fork has to be merged with every Postgres release. Moving to the extension APIs meant users get new Postgres features immediately and keep their existing drivers and tools.
Each shard is a regular table on a worker, so the workers’ own Postgres planner, indexes and storage do the local work, and Citus only has to plan across shards.

choices.choice: Colocate related tables by a shared distribution column
choices.why: Placing the shards that hold related rows of related tables on the same node lets joins, foreign keys and transactions for one tenant run on one machine without cross-node coordination.

choices.choice: A second model with one schema per shard
choices.why: Many multi-tenant apps already keep each tenant in its own schema and can’t add a tenant column to every table. Schema-based sharding scales them out with no query changes, at the cost of fewer tenants per node and no parallel cross-tenant queries.
